name: Who Pays for QC?
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Follow the Money: The Three Buyers Keeping Quantum Computing Alive
lesson.summary: With no mass commercial market yet, quantum computing survives on three overlapping sources of money, governments, corporate R&D budgets, and capital markets, each buying something different from an ordinary paying customer.
lesson.body:
Given the revenue model problem, an obvious question follows: if quantum computing companies are not selling a product that beats classical alternatives on a task customers need solved, who is actually paying them, and why do those payments keep flowing? The answer breaks down into three overlapping groups, each buying something other than a finished, superior product.

The first is governments, through research grants, national laboratory contracts, and defense-related funding. Governments are not primarily buying a working computer the way a business buys office software; they are buying strategic capability and hedging against being left behind on a technology with potential national security and economic implications, from code-breaking risk to future industrial advantage. That purchase logic tolerates a much longer payoff horizon and much more uncertainty than an ordinary commercial buyer would accept, which is exactly why government money, discussed in the funding pressure chapter, has been able to sustain the field through years without commercial revenue.

The second is large corporations with dedicated R&D exploration budgets, particularly in banking, pharmaceuticals, automotive, aerospace, and chemicals. These firms run pilot projects on problems like portfolio optimization, molecule simulation, or logistics routing, but the honest purpose of most of these engagements is to build internal expertise and maintain organizational readiness in case quantum computing eventually becomes useful, not to solve a production problem today. The cost of this kind of exploration is trivial relative to these companies' overall R&D budgets: cloud access to a quantum processor can run from a few dollars to a few hundred dollars per task depending on the hardware and provider, pocket change for a company with an R&D budget in the hundreds of millions or billions. That affordability matters, because it means large enterprises can sustain exploratory quantum spending indefinitely without that spending ever reflecting genuine operational need.

The third buyer is capital markets themselves, venture capitalists and public equity investors who are not purchasing a computation at all but a claim on a possible future payoff. This is a fundamentally different transaction from the other two: it is speculative capital allocation, priced on a story about what quantum computing might eventually be worth, rather than payment for value already delivered. It is the largest single category of money in the field's history and the most sensitive to shifts in sentiment, which is why chapters later in this section look closely at how that capital entered the market through vehicles like SPACs and how its expectations have collided with the industry's actual financial results.

These three sources of money overlap in practice more than the clean categories suggest. Government contracts often flow to the same corporate R&D labs running exploratory pilots, and capital markets price companies partly based on which government and corporate names appear in their announced partnership lists. That overlap is precisely what makes evaluating real customer demand difficult, since a partnership announcement might represent any of the three motives above, strategic hedging, cheap exploration, or narrative-building for investors, without clearly saying which. Sorting that out is the task of the next chapter.
